title: Blue-green, canary and feature flags
summary: Ways to release that let you see trouble before every user does.

steps.title: Recreate and rolling
body: The simplest strategies:
- **Recreate**: stop v1, start v2. Downtime in between. Fine for an internal tool at 3am, nothing else.
- **Rolling**: replace instances a few at a time behind the load balancer. No downtime, but for a while **v1 and v2 serve traffic together**,
so they must be compatible (same database schema, same API).
```text
rolling, 4 instances:   [v1 v1 v1 v1] → [v2 v1 v1 v1] → [v2 v2 v1 v1] → ... → [v2 v2 v2 v2]

steps.prompt: During a rolling deploy, users report that refreshing the page randomly shows old and new layouts. What is happening?
options: Requests are balanced across instances running v1 and v2 at the same time
The deploy failed and rolled back
steps.explain: That mixed state is inherent to rolling deploys; design changes to tolerate it (or use sticky sessions for the transition).

steps.title: Blue-green
body: Run **two complete environments**. Blue serves users; deploy v2 to green, test it privately, then switch the router.
```text
┌──► blue  (v1)   ← live
router ───────┤
└──► green (v2)   ← deployed, smoke-tested, idle
switch:  router → green.   rollback:  router → blue (seconds)
Pros: instant switch and instant rollback. Cons: double the infrastructure, and the **database is shared**, so schema changes still need care.

steps.prompt: With blue-green, green (v2) is live and errors spike. What is the rollback?
options: Point the router back at blue, which is still running v1
Rebuild v1 from source and deploy it to green
steps.explain: Blue was kept warm exactly for this: the switch back takes seconds and needs no build.

steps.title: Canary
body: Send a **small slice** of real traffic to v2, compare its error rate and latency with v1, and widen step by step:
```text
└ watch error rate, p95 latency at each step; any regression → back to 0%
Users must be **sticky**: the same user should always land on the same version, or they see features flicker. That is done by hashing
a stable id (user id, session cookie) into a bucket 0–99 and sending buckets below the percentage to the canary. Raising the percentage
only adds users; nobody already on the canary is moved back.

steps.prompt: Match each strategy to its main trade-off.
pairs: no extra servers, but two versions are live together
instant rollback, but double the infrastructure
real-traffic evidence, but needs good metrics and routing

steps.title: Feature flags
body: A **feature flag** separates *deploying* code from *releasing* a feature:
```csharp fragment
if (flags.IsEnabled("new-checkout", user))
return NewCheckout(cart);
return OldCheckout(cart);
The code ships dark, then the flag is turned on for staff, then 10% of users, then everyone, without a deploy. Turning it off is the fastest
rollback there is. The cost: every flag is a branch in your code; delete it once the rollout is done.

steps.prompt: Which tool fits each situation best?
items: let the sales team demo an unfinished feature to one customer
a new .NET runtime version: check real error rates on a small share of traffic
need to switch the whole site back in seconds after a big infrastructure change
turn off a misbehaving recommendation widget without deploying
gradually prove a new build under production load
test the complete new environment privately before any user sees it

steps.prompt: A canary is at 10%. User `u42` hashes to bucket 7, user `u77` to bucket 34. The canary is raised to 25%, then 50%. Which version does each user get at 50%? Type one line per user, like `u42 stable`.
steps.explain: 7 < 50 and 34 < 50. `u42` has been on the canary since 10%; `u77` joined at 50%.

steps.title: A sticky canary splitter
prompt: Write `string Route(string userId, int canaryPercent)` returning `"canary"` or `"stable"`.
Hash the user id with **32-bit FNV-1a** over its UTF-8 bytes:
for each byte b:  h = h XOR b;  h = h * 16777619   (uint arithmetic wraps)
The user's bucket is `h % 100`; buckets below `canaryPercent` go to the canary. Do not use `string.GetHashCode()`: it changes between
process runs, so users would not stay sticky.
hints: `h ^= b; h *= 16777619;` — uint multiplication wraps around automatically in an unchecked context.
template: Dojo.Eq("sticky: same answer twice", Route("bob", 30), Route("bob", 30));
Dojo.Check("about a quarter of 1000 users at 25%", dojoCount > 200 && dojoCount < 300, $"got {dojoCount}");
bool dojoMonotone = Enumerable.Range(0, 500).All(i => Route("user" + i, 10) == "stable" || Route("user" + i, 50) == "canary");
Dojo.Check("raising the percentage never moves a canary user back", dojoMonotone, "someone left the canary when it grew");
Dojo.Check("uses the FNV-1a hash", Route("a", 20) == "stable" && Route("a", 21) == "canary", "FNV-1a of \"a\" is 3826002220, so its bucket is 20; check your constants");
